schema.name: PowerShell
schema.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: PushNotification
tools.description:
This tool sends a desktop notification in the user's terminal. If Remote Control is connected, it also pushes to their phone. Either way, it pulls their attention from whatever they're doing — a meeting, another task, dinner — to this session. That's the cost. The benefit is they learn something now that they'd want to know now: a long task finished while they were away, a build is ready, you've hit something that needs their decision before you can continue.

Because a notification they didn't need is annoying in a way that accumulates, err toward not sending one. Don't notify for routine progress, or to announce you've answered something they asked seconds ago and are clearly still watching, or when a quick task completes. Notify when there's a real chance they've walked away and there's something worth coming back for — or when they've explicitly asked you to notify them.

Keep the message under 200 characters, one line, no markdown. Lead with what they'd act on — "build failed: 2 auth tests" tells them more than "task done" and more than a status dump.

When the user is actively at the terminal, your output already reaches them — a notification on top of it would be a duplicate, so the tool skips it and says so. A "not sent" result is expected and only ever about this one notification: it was redundant, turned off, or had nowhere to go.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: SendMessage
tools.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead.

- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

Now I have a full picture. Let me lay it out.

---

## Faust's Intel Report: `Phase_ESP32.md` + Codex of Time Status

### What I Understand from `Phase_ESP32.md`

This doc is **the hardware-backend interface contract** for **Universe 25 — Golden Hour Task Engine**. It defines a new operational mode for the ESP32: instead of just running timers from RFID cards, the device becomes a **live task terminal** connected to your local Python backend (port 8080).

**Three architectural pillars:**

| Pillar | What it means |
|--------|--------------|
| **Pure Task Execution** | No fake XP or coins. Completing a Google Task IS the reward — authentic productivity, zero synthetic inflation |
| **Triplet Focus Model** | The display shows exactly 3 tasks at a time. Navigate between them, pick one, destroy it |
| **Sub-2ms Local Cache** | The ESP32 never waits for Google. All reads/writes hit a local `tasks_cache.json` on your D:\ drive. Google sync happens silently in the background |

**Three API calls the ESP32 makes:**
1. `POST /sync` — Boot / manual button → pull all 18 Google Task lists into local cache
2. `GET /esp32/queue?limit=3` — Fetch the current Triplet (< 2ms, pure local disk)
3. `POST /complete` → Mark a task done (local cache update < 1ms, async Google PATCH in background)

**Hardware buttons specified in the spec:**
- `BTN_NEXT` (GPIO 18) — cycle through the 3 tasks
- `BTN_COMPLETE` (GPIO 19) — mark selected task as DONE

---

### What the Existing Codex of Time Firmware Is

The current `main.cpp` is a **complete, solid Arc 3 MVP**:
- Dual-SPI: HSPI for GC9A01 round display, VSPI for MFRC522 RFID
- 5-state machine: `IDLE_READY → CARD_DETECTED → TIMER_RUNNING → TIMER_FINISHED → ERROR`
- JQ8900 audio, LittleFS flash log, Method B RFID hard power-down
- **Wi-Fi is intentionally OFF** (`WiFi.mode(WIFI_OFF)`) — this is the LOCAL-ONLY MVP

---

### What We're About to Build: **Tab 2 — Golden Hour (Task Engine)**

The vision is the gear **switches between two tabs** (modes):
- **Tab 1 (existing):** `CLOCK-UP!` — RFID card → Timer → logged session
- **Tab 2 (new):** `GOLDEN HOUR` — Wi-Fi connect → fetch Triplet queue → navigate → complete tasks

A hardware button (or button combo) will **rotate between tabs on the display**, and each tab runs its own complete logic loop.

---

**My question before I design the architecture:** Do you want a **dedicated physical button** for tab switching, or should we use a **long-press** or **button combo** on existing hardware? The spec already claims GPIO 18 & 19 — do we have more GPIO available, or do we repurpose them based on which tab is active?

content.text:
That confirms it — **only one SSID visible, and it's 802.11ac on channel 120 (5 GHz only)**. The router is not broadcasting a 2.4 GHz band, or it's broadcasting under a different name that's out of range from the PC.

**The ESP32-WROOM-32 cannot connect to this. It has no 5 GHz radio. Full stop.**

### You have three options:

| Option | What to do | Effort |
|--------|-----------|--------|
| **A — Enable 2.4 GHz on the router** | Log into the router admin panel, enable the 2.4 GHz radio, give it an SSID (same or different name is fine) | Low — best long-term fix |
| **B — Mobile hotspot from your phone** | Enable hotspot on your phone (force 2.4 GHz mode), connect the ESP32 to that | Zero effort, good for testing right now |
| **C — PC shares its connection as a 2.4 GHz hotspot** | Windows → Settings → Mobile Hotspot → share over Wi-Fi (band: 2.4 GHz) | Low effort, works if your Intel AX200 can host |

---

### Fastest path right now: **Option B — Phone hotspot**

1. On your phone: **Settings → Hotspot → set band to 2.4 GHz**
2. Give it an SSID + password you control
3. Update `main.cpp` with the new credentials:

The only two lines that need to change are:

```cpp
#define WIFI_SSID       "YourPhoneHotspot"
#define WIFI_PASSWORD   "YourHotspotPass"
```

But your **backend is on `192.168.2.16`** — when the ESP32 is on the phone hotspot, it will be on a different subnet and **cannot reach that IP**. So if you go with Option B, you also need to either:
- Run the backend on the phone (not practical), or  
- **Use Option C instead** — share the PC's own internet via a Windows hotspot, so both the ESP32 and the backend are on the same machine

---

### Recommended: Option C — Windows Mobile Hotspot

This keeps both devices on the same subnet (your PC assigns the ESP32 an IP, the backend is `localhost` or `192.168.137.1` — the default Windows hotspot gateway).

content.text:
Based on my research, here are the accurate technical answers for ESP32 connectivity options:

## 1. ESP32 Classic Bluetooth PAN (BNEP) - ❌ NOT SUPPORTED

**Current Status:** ESP32's Bluedroid stack does **NOT** support the PAN profile or BNEP protocol.

- The ESP-IDF Bluedroid implementation supports A2DP, AVRCP, HFP, SPP, and HID profiles
- PAN/BNEP is **not implemented** in the official stack
- Multiple GitHub issues (#3245, #7767) have requested this feature with no official implementation
- Android's Bluetooth tethering requires the device to act as a PANU (PAN User) role with BNEP (RFC 3006) support
- **Conclusion:** You cannot use ESP32 Classic Bluetooth to connect to Android's Bluetooth tethering

## 2. ESP32 BLE Internet Sharing - ⚠️ NO NATIVE SUPPORT

**Current Status:** Not possible without a custom Android companion app.

Android does not natively support internet sharing over BLE at the OS level. Potential approaches:

- **IPSP/6LoWPAN (RFC 7668):** Theoretically possible but requires root/custom Android OS - not practical
- **Custom L2CAP CoC Proxy:** Requires a custom Android app (Android 10+) to proxy traffic over BLE L2CAP channels
  - Speed: ~100-300 kbps
  - ESP32 side: Custom `esp_netif` driver bridging BLE to lwIP stack
- **Custom GATT Proxy:** Even slower (~10-60 kbps), requires Android app to handle HTTP/MQTT requests

**Conclusion:** BLE internet sharing requires significant custom development on both ESP32 and Android sides with no out-of-the-box solution.

## 3. Android Hotspot Static/Reserved IP - ❌ NOT SUPPORTED (Stock)

**Current Status:** Native Android hotspot does NOT support MAC-based DHCP reservations.

- Stock Android hotspot (all versions through Android 14) lacks UI for static IP assignment by MAC address
- **Workarounds:**
  - **Easiest:** Configure static IP on the ESP32 client side (not MAC-based, but achieves consistency)
  - **Rooted Android:** Edit `/data/misc/dhcp/dnsmasq.conf` to add `dhcp-host=c0:cd:d6:ca:04:c8,192.168.43.100`
  - **Third-party apps:** Require root access for true MAC reservation

**Conclusion:** For your MAC address (c0:cd:d6:ca:04:c8), set a static IP on the ESP32 side instead.

## 4. Windows ICS over USB (RNDIS) - ✅ POSSIBLE

**Current Status:** Works with ESP32-S2/S3 (native USB support).

- **ESP32-S2/S3** can enumerate as a USB RNDIS network adapter using TinyUSB
- Windows recognizes it as "Remote NDIS Compatible Device"
- Enable ICS on your main Windows internet adapter, sharing to the RNDIS adapter
- **Default ICS subnet:** `192.168.137.x` (Windows host at `192.168.137.1`)
- **ESP-IDF examples:** `examples/peripherals/usb/device/tusb_rndis` or `tusb_ncm`
- **Note:** NCM (Network Control Model) is now preferred over RNDIS on Windows 10/11 for better stability

**Limitation:** Original ESP32 (without native USB) cannot do this - only ESP32-S2/S3.

**Conclusion:** This is practical and works well if you're using ESP32-S2 or ESP32-S3.

## 5. Android Hotspot Gateway IP - ✅ HISTORICALLY 192.168.43.1

**Current Status:** Mostly consistent but not guaranteed on Android 10+.

- **Android 2.x through 9.x:** Gateway is **consistently 192.168.43.1**
- **Subnet:** `192.168.43.0/24`, DHCP range usually `.10` to `.254`
- **Android 10+:** Google introduced randomization for privacy
  - Many manufacturers (Samsung, Xiaomi, OnePlus) still default to `192.168.43.1`
  - Stock Android (Pixel) may use alternative subnets: `192.168.0.x`, `192.168.1.x`, or `10.0.0.x`

**Best Practice for ESP32 Arduino:**
```cpp
// Don't hardcode - use DHCP and query the gateway
WiFi.begin(ssid, password);
IPAddress gateway = WiFi.gatewayIP(); // Gets actual gateway dynamically
```

**Conclusion:** `192.168.43.1` is the most common gateway IP, but for robust code, always query the gateway via DHCP rather than hardcoding.

---

## Summary Recommendations

For reliable ESP32 internet connectivity via phone/PC:

1. **Best option:** Connect ESP32 to Android hotspot via WiFi (query gateway dynamically)
2. **Static IP workaround:** Configure static IP on ESP32 side since Android doesn't support MAC reservations
3. **USB option:** Use ESP32-S2/S3 with RNDIS/NCM + Windows ICS if USB connection is acceptable
4. **Avoid:** Bluetooth Classic PAN (not supported) and BLE internet sharing (too complex, no native support)

- **IPSP/6LoWPAN (RFC 7668):** Theoretically possible but requires root/custom Android OS - not practical
- **Custom L2CAP CoC Proxy:** Requires a custom Android app (Android 10+) to proxy traffic over BLE L2CAP channels
  - Speed: ~100-300 kbps
  - ESP32 side: Custom `esp_netif` driver bridging BLE to lwIP stack
- **Custom GATT Proxy:** Even slower (~10-60 kbps), requires Android app to handle HTTP/MQTT requests

**Conclusion:** BLE internet sharing requires significant custom development on both ESP32 and Android sides with no out-of-the-box solution.

## 3. Android Hotspot Static/Reserved IP - ❌ NOT SUPPORTED (Stock)

**Current Status:** Native Android hotspot does NOT support MAC-based DHCP reservations.

- Stock Android hotspot (all versions through Android 14) lacks UI for static IP assignment by MAC address
- **Workarounds:**
  - **Easiest:** Configure static IP on the ESP32 client side (not MAC-based, but achieves consistency)
  - **Rooted Android:** Edit `/data/misc/dhcp/dnsmasq.conf` to add `dhcp-host=c0:cd:d6:ca:04:c8,192.168.43.100`
  - **Third-party apps:** Require root access for true MAC reservation

**Conclusion:** For your MAC address (c0:cd:d6:ca:04:c8), set a static IP on the ESP32 side instead.

## 4. Windows ICS over USB (RNDIS) - ✅ POSSIBLE

**Current Status:** Works with ESP32-S2/S3 (native USB support).

- **ESP32-S2/S3** can enumerate as a USB RNDIS network adapter using TinyUSB
- Windows recognizes it as "Remote NDIS Compatible Device"
- Enable ICS on your main Windows internet adapter, sharing to the RNDIS adapter
- **Default ICS subnet:** `192.168.137.x` (Windows host at `192.168.137.1`)
- **ESP-IDF examples:** `examples/peripherals/usb/device/tusb_rndis` or `tusb_ncm`
- **Note:** NCM (Network Control Model) is now preferred over RNDIS on Windows 10/11 for better stability

**Limitation:** Original ESP32 (without native USB) cannot do this - only ESP32-S2/S3.

**Conclusion:** This is practical and works well if you're using ESP32-S2 or ESP32-S3.

## 5. Android Hotspot Gateway IP - ✅ HISTORICALLY 192.168.43.1

**Current Status:** Mostly consistent but not guaranteed on Android 10+.

- **Android 2.x through 9.x:** Gateway is **consistently 192.168.43.1**
- **Subnet:** `192.168.43.0/24`, DHCP range usually `.10` to `.254`
- **Android 10+:** Google introduced randomization for privacy
  - Many manufacturers (Samsung, Xiaomi, OnePlus) still default to `192.168.43.1`
  - Stock Android (Pixel) may use alternative subnets: `192.168.0.x`, `192.168.1.x`, or `10.0.0.x`

**Best Practice for ESP32 Arduino:**
```cpp
// Don't hardcode - use DHCP and query the gateway
WiFi.begin(ssid, password);
IPAddress gateway = WiFi.gatewayIP(); // Gets actual gateway dynamically
```

**Conclusion:** `192.168.43.1` is the most common gateway IP, but for robust code, always query the gateway via DHCP rather than hardcoding.

---

## Summary Recommendations

For reliable ESP32 internet connectivity via phone/PC:

1. **Best option:** Connect ESP32 to Android hotspot via WiFi (query gateway dynamically)
2. **Static IP workaround:** Configure static IP on ESP32 side since Android doesn't support MAC reservations
3. **USB option:** Use ESP32-S2/S3 with RNDIS/NCM + Windows ICS if USB connection is acceptable
4. **Avoid:** Bluetooth Classic PAN (not supported) and BLE internet sharing (too complex, no native support)

Here's the full picture, straight:

---

## Bluetooth tethering — **dead end**

The ESP32's Bluetooth stack does not implement the PAN/BNEP profile. Bluetooth tethering from an Android phone requires exactly that. It is not supported and there is no workaround in the Arduino framework. Not going there.

---

## The actual solution: **Phone hotspot + static IP on the ESP32 side**

The "inconsistent IP" problem you're worried about is the **ESP32's assigned IP**, which does change. But the thing that matters for us is the **opposite direction** — the **backend is on your PC**, so what needs to be consistent is **your PC's IP on the hotspot subnet**.

Here's the key insight the research surfaced:

> **When the ESP32 connects to Android hotspot via DHCP, we can query `WiFi.gatewayIP()` at runtime — that always points to the phone. The backend is on the PC, not the phone.**

So the real problem is: **your PC's IP on the hotspot subnet is dynamic**. We solve that by assigning your PC a static IP on the hotspot interface.

### The plan:

```
[Phone Hotspot 2.4GHz]
        │
        ├── ESP32  ←── DHCP (its IP doesn't matter, it's the client)
        │
        └── PC  ←── Static IP: 192.168.43.100 (we fix this in Windows)
                     Backend runs on: http://192.168.43.100:8080
```

**Steps:**

1. **Enable hotspot on your phone** — Settings → Hotspot → force **2.4 GHz band** (critical)
2. **On your PC**: Settings → Network → find the hotspot adapter → set **static IP `192.168.43.100`**, subnet `255.255.255.0`, gateway `192.168.43.1`
3. **Update firmware**: change `BACKEND_HOST` to `http://192.168.43.100:8080`
4. **Connect your PC to the phone hotspot** so the backend is reachable on that IP

`192.168.43.1` is the standard Android hotspot gateway and is consistent across virtually all Android manufacturers. Your PC gets a fixed IP we assign, so it never drifts.

---

**Bluetooth tethering** — dead end, ESP32 stack doesn't support it. Not going there.

**mDNS (`.local` hostname)** — works on home routers, **fails on phone hotspot** due to multicast blocking. Also dead end for this use case.

```
PC Backend                          ESP32
    │                                  │

    │                                  │
    │                   stores IP ─────┘
    │◀── GET /esp32/queue ─────────────│
    │──▶ { tasks: [...] } ────────────▶│
```

from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware

    if p not in sys.path:

    if BASE_DIR.exists():
        for proj_dir in BASE_DIR.iterdir():
            log_dir = proj_dir / "logs"

# backend/core/udp_beacon.py — Faust UDP Beacon
# Broadcasts the backend's current IP on a known port every 5 seconds.
# The ESP32 listens on boot, catches the IP, uses it for all HTTP calls.
# This eliminates hardcoded IPs entirely — works across any network.

import socket
import threading
import time

BEACON_PORT    = 4210
BEACON_INTERVAL = 5   # seconds between broadcasts
BACKEND_PORT   = 8080
BEACON_PREFIX  = "FAUST-SERVER"


def _get_local_ip() -> str:
    """Resolve the machine's outbound IP without actually sending packets."""
    try:
        s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
        s.connect(("8.8.8.8", 80))
        ip = s.getsockname()[0]
        s.close()
        return ip
    except Exception:
        return "127.0.0.1"


def _beacon_loop(stop_event: threading.Event) -> None:
    sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
    sock.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_BROADCAST, 1)
    sock.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)

    print(f"[UDP BEACON] Started — broadcasting on port {BEACON_PORT} every {BEACON_INTERVAL}s")

    while not stop_event.is_set():
        ip = _get_local_ip()
        message = f"{BEACON_PREFIX}:{ip}:{BACKEND_PORT}".encode()

        try:
            sock.sendto(message, ("<broadcast>", BEACON_PORT))
            print(f"[UDP BEACON] {message.decode()}")
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"[UDP BEACON] Send error: {e}")

        stop_event.wait(BEACON_INTERVAL)

    sock.close()
    print("[UDP BEACON] Stopped.")


class UDPBeacon:
    """Lifecycle-managed UDP beacon. Call start() / stop()."""

    def __init__(self):
        self._stop_event = threading.Event()
        self._thread: threading.Thread | None = None

    def start(self):
        self._stop_event.clear()
        self._thread = threading.Thread(
            target=_beacon_loop,
            args=(self._stop_event,),
            daemon=True,
            name="udp-beacon"
        )
        self._thread.start()

    def stop(self):
        self._stop_event.set()
        if self._thread:
            self._thread.join(timeout=BEACON_INTERVAL + 1)

Now everything clicks into place. 

With a **Cloudflare Tunnel**, the backend has a **fixed public domain** (e.g., `https://api.yourdomain.com`). The ESP32 is purely an **outbound client** making HTTPS/HTTP requests — so **the ESP32's local IP and the phone's internal subnet do not matter at all.**

The only real challenge is: **Making the phone a rock-solid, zero-maintenance Wi-Fi tether for the gear that's always in your pocket.**

---

### Why Phone Hotspot Normally Feels Flaky (and how we solve each one)

```
┌─────────────────────────┐          2.4 GHz Wi-Fi          ┌─────────────────────────┐
│     Your Smartphone     │ ◀─────────────────────────────▶ │     ESP32 (Codex)       │
│  (Always near the gear) │                                 │  (Pocket/Wrist Actuator)│
└────────────┬────────────┘                                 └────────────┬────────────┘
             │ Cellular (4G/5G)                                          │ Outbound HTTPS
             ▼                                                           ▼
┌─────────────────────────┐                                 ┌─────────────────────────┐
│    Cloudflare Edge      │ ◀───────────────────────────────┤   Cloudflare Tunnel     │
│   (Fixed Public URL)    │                                 │   (Desktop Backend)     │
└─────────────────────────┘                                 └─────────────────────────┘
```

Here are the 4 failure points of phone hotspots and the exact fixes:

---

### 1. The 5 GHz Trap (Why it failed earlier)
* **Problem**: Most modern phones default to 5 GHz Wi-Fi hotspot. The ESP32-WROOM-32 has a **2.4 GHz radio only**.
* **Fix (Phone setting — do once)**:
  - **Android**: *Settings → Hotspot & Tethering → Wi-Fi Hotspot → AP Band* → Select **`2.4 GHz`** (or "Extend compatibility").
  - **iOS**: *Settings → Personal Hotspot* → Enable **`Maximize Compatibility`** (this forces 2.4 GHz broadcast).

---

### 2. The Android "Auto-Sleep / Power Saver" Shutdown
* **Problem**: When traffic pauses for a few minutes, Android automatically turns off the hotspot to save battery, dropping the ESP32.
* **Fix (Phone setting — do once)**:
  - *Hotspot Settings → Turn off hotspot automatically / Timeout* → Set to **`Never`** (or "Always on").
  - *Settings → Battery Optimization / App Info (Tethering/Settings)* → Set to **`Unrestricted` / `Don't Optimize`**.

---

### 3. Hotspot Drop / Reconnect Handling (Firmware side)
* **Problem**: When you toggle airplane mode, leave home, or the phone drops signal temporarily, standard ESP32 code hangs in an infinite `while` loop or needs a hard power cycle.
* **Fix (Firmware)**:
  - We configure `WiFi.setAutoReconnect(true)` and a non-blocking background watchdog.
  - If the phone hotspot drops for 10 seconds, the display shows a subtle `RECONNECTING...` HUD indicator while retrying in the background. As soon as the phone is back, it re-latches in `< 1s` without rebooting the ESP32 or freezing the UI/timer.

---

### 4. Background Keep-Alive Heartbeat
* **Problem**: Hotspots drop devices that don't transmit packets.
* **Fix (Firmware)**:
  - The ESP32 sends a tiny background heartbeat (or task queue refresh) every 60–120s. This keeps the phone's DHCP lease active and prevents the phone from killing the connection.

---

### Summary Checklist for You

1. **On your phone**:
   - Turn on Hotspot.
   - Set AP Band to **`2.4 GHz`** (or "Maximize Compatibility").
   - Set Hotspot Auto-Off/Timeout to **`Never`**.
   - Note the exact SSID and Password.

2. **Backend**:
   - Give me the **Cloudflare Tunnel URL** (or domain) when you have it ready.

Once you set your phone's hotspot to 2.4 GHz, tell me your hotspot SSID & password (and the Cloudflare tunnel URL if ready), and I will flash the bulletproof auto-reconnect firmware onto the Codex.

import serial, time
p = serial.Serial('COM4', 115200, timeout=0.5)

  2. Standard GFXfonts only contain ASCII glyphs (0x20–0x7E), lacking Vietnamese diacritics
  
  ### Solutions for Vietnamese on Adafruit_GFX
  
  #### **Solution A: U8g2_for_Adafruit_GFX (Recommended)**
  This library overlays U8g2's UTF-8 engine and Vietnamese fonts onto any Adafruit_GFX-compatible display.
  
  **Built-in Vietnamese Fonts:**
  - `u8g2_font_unifont_t_vietnamese1` / `vietnamese2` (16px)
  - `u8g2_font_cu12_t_vietnamese1` (12px compact)
  
  **Pros:**
  - Drop-in solution, no font conversion needed
  - Works with GC9A01 via Adafruit_GFX or Arduino_GFX
  - UTF-8 decoding handled automatically
  
  **Cons:**
  - Bitmap fonts only (no anti-aliasing)
  - Limited size/style options
  - Adds ~40-60KB to firmware
  
  **Implementation for GC9A01:**
  ```cpp
  #include <Arduino_GFX_Library.h>
  #include <U8g2_for_Adafruit_GFX.h>
  
  Arduino_DataBus *bus = new Arduino_ESP32SPI(TFT_DC, TFT_CS, 18, 23, -1);
  Arduino_GFX *gfx = new Arduino_GC9A01(bus, TFT_RST, 0, true);
  U8G2_FOR_ADAFRUIT_GFX u8g2Fonts;
  
  void setup() {
    gfx->begin();
    u8g2Fonts.begin(*gfx);
    u8g2Fonts.setFont(u8g2_font_unifont_t_vietnamese1);
    u8g2Fonts.setCursor(10, 50);
    u8g2Fonts.print("Xin chào Việt Nam!"); // UTF-8 works directly
  }
  ```
  
  #### **Solution B: Custom GFXfont with Vietnamese Glyphs**
  Convert a TTF font to GFXfont format including Vietnamese Unicode ranges:
  - Use `fontconvert` tool (Adafruit_GFX/fontconvert)
  - Include ranges: `0x0020-0x007E, 0x00C0-0x00FF, 0x0100-0x017F, 0x01A0-0x01B4, 0x1EA0-0x1EF9`
  
  **Pros:**
  - Custom styling
  - Integrates with existing Adafruit_GFX code
  
  **Cons:**
  - Manual UTF-8 decoding required (write custom `printUTF8()` wrapper)
  - Large font files (2-byte/3-byte UTF-8 = 134+ Vietnamese glyphs)
  - Complex build process
  
  ---
  
  ## 2. TFT_eSPI with GC9A01: Superior Alternative
  
  ### TFT_eSPI Native Support
  **YES**, TFT_eSPI has built-in GC9A01 driver support and offers smooth anti-aliased Vietnamese fonts.
  
  **Configuration (`User_Setup.h` or PlatformIO):**
  ```cpp
  #define GC9A01_DRIVER
  #define TFT_WIDTH  240
  #define TFT_HEIGHT 240
  #define TFT_MOSI 23
  #define TFT_SCLK 18
  #define TFT_CS   15
  #define TFT_DC   2
  #define TFT_RST  4
  #define SPI_FREQUENCY 27000000
  ```
  
  ### Vietnamese Smooth Fonts (.vlw)
  TFT_eSPI supports **anti-aliased smooth fonts** with Vietnamese:
  
  **Steps:**
  1. Use Processing sketch `Create_Font` (in TFT_eSPI/Tools) or online VLW generator
  2. Select a TTF font (e.g., Roboto, Noto Sans)
  3. Include Unicode ranges: `0x0020-0x1EF9` (covers all Vietnamese)
  4. Save `.vlw` to ESP32 SPIFFS/LittleFS
  5. Load and render:
  
  ```cpp
  #include <TFT_eSPI.h>
  #include <LittleFS.h>
  
  TFT_eSPI tft = TFT_eSPI();
  
  void setup() {
    LittleFS.begin();
    tft.init();
    tft.loadFont("Roboto_Vietnamese_24", LittleFS);
    tft.drawString("Xin chào Việt Nam!", 20, 40); // UTF-8 native
    tft.unloadFont();
  }
  ```
  
  **Pros:**
  - Smooth anti-aliased rendering
  - Native UTF-8 support
  - Faster than Adafruit_GFX (DMA support)
  - Multiple font sizes from one TTF
  
  **Cons:**
  - `.vlw` files consume flash storage (50-200KB per font size)
  - Requires SPIFFS/LittleFS setup
  
  ---
  
  ## 3. Lightweight Solutions for Vietnamese Diacritics
  
  ### Option 1: ASCII Conversion (No Diacritics)
  Strip Vietnamese tones for simple displays where accents aren't critical.
  
  ### Option 2: U8g2 Standalone
  If not committed to Adafruit_GFX, U8g2 library directly supports GC9A01 and Vietnamese fonts with lower overhead than the bridge library.
  
  ### Option 3: LovyanGFX
  Modern drop-in replacement supporting TTF fonts loaded directly from flash:
  ```cpp
  #include <LovyanGFX.hpp>
  lcd.loadFont("/vietnamese.ttf", LittleFS);
  lcd.drawString("Xin chào!", 10, 10);
  ```

  ```cpp
  //                        é è ẻ ẽ ẹ ê ế ề ể ễ ệ

  //                        ý ỳ ỷ ỹ ỵ

  String removeVietnameseDiacritics(const String &text) {
    String result = "";

        else if (codepoint >= 0x011C && codepoint <= 0x0123) result += (codepoint % 2 == 0) ? 'G' : 'g'; // Ĝ-ģ
        else if (codepoint >= 0x0124 && codepoint <= 0x0127) result += (codepoint % 2 == 0) ? 'H' : 'h'; // Ĥ-ħ
        else if (codepoint >= 0x0128 && codepoint <= 0x0131) result += (codepoint % 2 == 0) ? 'I' : 'i'; // Ĩ-ı
        else if (codepoint >= 0x0134 && codepoint <= 0x0135) result += (codepoint % 2 == 0) ? 'J' : 'j'; // Ĵ-ĵ
        else if (codepoint >= 0x0139 && codepoint <= 0x0142) result += (codepoint % 2 == 1) ? 'L' : 'l'; // Ĺ-ł
        else if (codepoint >= 0x0143 && codepoint <= 0x0148) result += (codepoint % 2 == 1) ? 'N' : 'n'; // Ń-ň
        else if (codepoint >= 0x014C && codepoint <= 0x0151) result += (codepoint % 2 == 0) ? 'O' : 'o'; // Ō-ő
        else if (codepoint >= 0x0154 && codepoint <= 0x0159) result += (codepoint % 2 == 0) ? 'R' : 'r'; // Ŕ-ř
        else if (codepoint >= 0x015A && codepoint <= 0x0161) result += (codepoint % 2 == 0) ? 'S' : 's'; // Ś-š
        else if (codepoint >= 0x0162 && codepoint <= 0x0167) result += (codepoint % 2 == 0) ? 'T' : 't'; // Ţ-ŧ

        else if (codepoint >= 0x0174 && codepoint <= 0x0175) result += (codepoint % 2 == 0) ? 'W' : 'w'; // Ŵ-ŵ

          if (codepoint >= 0x1EA0 && codepoint <= 0x1EB7) {
            result += (codepoint % 2 == 0) ? 'A' : 'a';
          }
          // E with tones
          else if (codepoint >= 0x1EB8 && codepoint <= 0x1EC7) {
            result += (codepoint % 2 == 0) ? 'E' : 'e';
          }
          // I with tones
          else if (codepoint >= 0x1EC8 && codepoint <= 0x1ECB) {
            result += (codepoint % 2 == 0) ? 'I' : 'i';
          }
          // O with tones and modifiers
          else if (codepoint >= 0x1ECC && codepoint <= 0x1EE3) {
            result += (codepoint % 2 == 0) ? 'O' : 'o';
          }
          // U with tones and modifiers
          else if (codepoint >= 0x1EE4 && codepoint <= 0x1EF1) {
            result += (codepoint % 2 == 0) ? 'U' : 'u';
          }
          // Y with tones
          else if (codepoint >= 0x1EF2 && codepoint <= 0x1EF9) {
            result += (codepoint % 2 == 0) ? 'Y' : 'y';
  ```

  This function correctly handles:
